🤿 Deep dive · Lesson 7 · 2 min read

How Computers See

How a picture turns into numbers, and how a network finds edges, shapes and objects in them.

A picture is a grid of numbers

To a computer, a photo is not a cat or a face. It is a grid of tiny squares called pixels, and each pixel is just a number. In a greyscale (black-and-white) picture, 0 means black, 255 means white, and the numbers in between are shades of grey. A colour pixel has three numbers: how much red, green and blue light it has (RGB). A 12-megapixel phone photo has about 12 million pixels: about 36 million numbers.

Did you know? MNIST, a famous dataset for teaching computers to read handwriting, has 70,000 pictures of handwritten digits. Each one is only 28 × 28 pixels: 784 numbers per digit.

Filters find patterns

How do you find an edge in a grid of numbers? Take a small grid of numbers, a filter (for example 3 × 3), and slide it over the picture, square by square. At each spot, multiply each number under the filter by the filter's number on top of it, and add everything up. Where the picture has an edge like the one the filter looks for, the sum is big. Where everything is one colour, it is zero or close to it. This sliding and adding is called a convolution.

Did you know? A blur filter has nine equal numbers, each 1/9. So every new pixel is the average of itself and its eight neighbours, and sharp edges get soft. Photo apps use filters like this all the time.

Layers build up

A convolutional neural network (CNN) uses many filters, in layers. Nobody writes these filters by hand: the network learns their numbers from large sets of labelled photos. The first layer usually finds simple edges and spots of colour. The next layers combine them into corners and textures, then into parts like eyes or wheels, and the last layers into whole objects: “cat”, “bicycle”, “stop sign”. In 2012 a CNN called AlexNet won ImageNet, a contest to sort photos into 1,000 categories, by a wide margin, and helped start the deep learning boom.

Where it works, and where it fails

Computer vision unlocks phones with your face, helps doctors spot problems in medical scans, reads number plates and helps cars see the road. But it finds patterns, not meaning. Bad lighting, an unusual angle or a picture unlike its training photos can confuse it. Researchers have even found adversarial examples: tiny, carefully chosen changes to a picture, invisible to people, that make a model see something completely different.

Did you know? In a well-known 2014 experiment, researchers added a faint pattern of noise to a photo of a panda. People still saw a panda, but the network said “gibbon”, and was very sure of it. Later, others showed that a few stickers on a stop sign could make a model misread the sign. That's why systems where safety is at stake are tested very carefully.

Key points

  • To a computer, a picture is a grid of numbers: one per pixel, or three for colour (RGB).
  • A filter slides over the picture and adds up products (a convolution); a CNN learns its own filters from examples.
  • Vision models see patterns, not meaning: lighting, odd angles and adversarial examples can fool them.

Check yourself

A network has learned to recognise stop signs. Which of these could fool it?

Show the answer

Right answer: A few small stickers, cleverly placed on the sign

Researchers showed that a few well-placed stickers can make a model misread a stop sign: an adversarial example. Good daylight is exactly what the model learned from, and a slightly bigger photo has the same patterns, so neither of those is a problem.
